extracted.intended_audience: lawyers, judges, military legal officers, and legal researchers working on military/war powers and related statutory interpretation
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and records authoritative definitions, holdings, and interpretive rules from a legal reference on war powers, martial law, and related military law topics. Useful for legal practitioners and scholars needing standards and precedent about when war exists/ends, scope of military authority, and constructions of key terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspension of the writ of habeas corpus / martial law proclamations
rubrics_metrics.description: Executive proclamations (Sept. 24, 1862; Sept. 15, 1863; Dec. 1, 1865; Apr. 2, 1866) suspended the writ of habeas corpus as to certain classes of persons and placed certain areas (e.g., District of Columbia) under martial law for specified periods; revocations and exceptions were effected by later proclamations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original text describes that proclamations suspended the writ 'during the rebellion' as to certain classes, and that revoking proclamations excepted particular States/Territories. The holdings treat the dates of proclamations as determinative of the temporal scope of martial law for jurisdictional purposes (e.g., martial law in D.C. considered to have existed from Sept. 24, 1862 to Apr. 2, 1866 for indicated classes). Citations: R. So, 177, Feb. 1874 and related proclamations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Military aid to States for domestic violence (command and control rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the United States protects a State against 'domestic violence', its military forces act in aid of State authorities to the extent necessary to reestablish civil authority, but the forces remain under federal command (their military officers under the President), not under State command.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establishes that federal military forces are an independent force operating under Presidential orders to perform constitutional duties to the State; they are not placed under State authority. Citation: C. 8383, May, 1900.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial deference on termination of war
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts will not, as an original matter, determine whether a war has terminated; the judiciary should await and abide by the action of the President or Congress on such questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Holding arises in a case where a State judge discharged a soldier on grounds the war had ended. The rule is that such political determinations are for the executive/congressional branches. Citation: R. 18, 293, Oct., 1865.

rubrics_metrics.name: End of war by exchange of treaty ratifications
rubrics_metrics.description: For treaty terminations (e.g., Spanish–American War), the status of war terminates on the date when ratifications of the peace treaty are exchanged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied to the war between Spain and the United States; multiple examiner citations listed (C. 12^88 Apr. 29, 1902; others). Also supported by other authorities (e.g., ex parte Ortiz).

rubrics_metrics.name: Presidential proclamation can fix end of war in specific territories
rubrics_metrics.description: A presidential proclamation declaring that insurrection is at an end can fix the termination date of war status for specified territories (example: Philippine Archipelago except Moro country declared at peace by July 4, 1902 proclamation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Holding: war status in the Philippines (except Moro country) terminated on date of publication of the proclamation (July 4, 1902). Citations: C. 13743, Dec. 2, 1902; others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Military order can fix termination date of hostilities (China example)
rubrics_metrics.description: A military General Order (No. 19, Hq. China Relief Expedition) fixing a date may be treated as determinative of the date hostilities ended in that theater (example: war in China ended May 12, 1901).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citation: C. 17609, Mar. 22, 1905. Use when determining theater-specific termination of war for legal/status consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: War correspondents: noncombatant status and command jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: War correspondents are noncombatants within a theater of military occupation but fall within the jurisdiction of the commanding general of the army which they accompany; the commanding general may issue rules/regulations governing their conduct while within his command.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affirms noncombatant status but subjects correspondents to military regulation within command limits. Citation: C. 16351, May 19, 1904.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and limits of 'authorized confinement' under Article IV (G.O. 16/Art. IV)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Authorized confinement' is not limited to the maximum authorized term; confinement for a period less than the maximum is also authorized. However, such confinement is limited to the specific confinement authorized by the Article II or, if not provided, by custom — it may not be increased by substituting confinement for forfeiture or on account of previous convictions unless provided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifies how sentencing options operate: courts may adjudge confinement less than the statutory maximum and cannot increase confinement by substituting confinement for forfeiture or for prior convictions unless that is specifically authorized. Citation: C. 8548, July, 1900; also C. 1551, July, 1895.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Day' in maximum punishment orders
rubrics_metrics.description: When 'day' or 'days' are used in a maximum punishment order, they refer to a day of twenty-four hours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifies temporal measurement for punishment orders in military context. Citation: P. 53, 149, Apr., 1892.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Month' construed as calendar month in sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'month' or 'months' used in a sentence is to be construed as meaning calendar month(s), abandoning the older doctrine that it meant lunar month in court-martial sentences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives the current rule of statutory construction for military sentences: calendar months are used as commonly in American statute construction. Citation: R. 26, 374, Jan., 1868.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of 'authorized' and 'authorized to exercise' powers (interpretive cross-reference)
rubrics_metrics.description: The right to exercise one power (e.g., to suspend the writ) implies the right to exercise related powers (e.g., proclaim martial law); statutory and precedent authorities treat such powers as interconnected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text notes that the power to suspend the writ and to proclaim martial law include one another; see Am. Law Reg. and ex parte Field. Use this principle when construing executive wartime powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions of specific military/legal terms (lexicographic holdings)
rubrics_metrics.description: Authoritative short definitions or constructions for many terms used in military law (examples include 'accouterments', 'court of justice', 'active duty', 'active service', 'actual service', 'civil office', 'civil war', 'competent authority', 'corps', 'crimes', 'day/month', 'disbursing officer', 'embezzlement', 'enlistment', 'flag', 'forfeiture', 'grant/license', 'military stores', 'mutiny', 'war', etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each listed term is tied to a short holding or definition and cross-references to fuller discussion elsewhere in the treatise. Examples provided in text: 'Accouterments' applies to parts of soldier's personal equipment issued by Ordnance Dept (belts, cartridge pouches); 'Officer' (superior officer) means commissioned officer for article application; 'Reputable person' example: a man trading illicitly with soldiers is not 'reputable' to witness transfers. These definitions function as binding interpretive rules in military-adjacent litigation and administrative actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretive rule: 'may' can be construed as 'must/shall' in statutory context
rubrics_metrics.description: In certain statutory contexts the word 'may' can be equivalent to 'must' or 'shall' (specific example referenced in river and harbor act and general laws constructions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise cites examples where 'may' is construed as mandatory depending on statute framing and context (see Laws I B 1 a; Navigable waters X A 1). Apply careful statutory-contextual analysis to determine permissive vs. mandatory meaning.
